option_a: cause a venturi effect which energizes the boundary layer.
option_b: allow space for vibration of the slat.
option_d: slow the air flow in the slot so that more pressure is created under the wing.
explanation: The slot between an extended slat and the wing leading edge channels high-energy air from the lower surface to the upper surface, energizing the boundary layer and postponing flow separation.

question_text: A deployed slat will:
option_a: increase the boundary layer energy, move the suction peak from the fixed part of the wing to the slat, so that the stall is postponed to higher angles of attack.
option_b: increase the boundary layer energy and increase the suction peak on the fixed part of the wing, so that the stall is postponed to higher angles of attack.
option_c: decrease the boundary layer energy and decrease the suction peak on the slat, so that CLmax is reached at lower angles of attack.
option_d: increase the camber of the aerofoil and increase the effective angle of attack, so that CLmax is reached at higher angles of attack.
explanation: Slats form a slot that channels high-energy air to the upper surface of the wing, which energizes the boundary layer and moves the suction peak from the wing leading edge onto the slat itself, delaying the stall.

question_text: What increases the stalling angle of attack ? Use of :
option_d: fuselage mounted speed-brakes
explanation: Slats are designed to energize the boundary layer and delay airflow separation, which directly increases the stalling (critical) angle of attack.

question_text: The use of a slot in the leading edge of the wing enables the aeroplane to fly at a slower speed because :
option_a: it delays the stall to a higher angle of attack
option_b: the laminar part of the boundary layer gets thicker
option_c: it decelerates the upper surface boundary layer air
option_d: it changes the camber of the wing
explanation: A leading edge slot allows high-energy air to flow over the upper surface of the wing, which delays boundary layer separation (stall) to a higher angle of attack, permitting flight at slower airspeeds.

question_text: (For this question use annex 081-6271A)The high lift device shown in the figure is a
option_d: Krueger flap
explanation: The high-lift device shown is a leading edge slat, which slides forward on tracks to create a slot that energizes the upper surface boundary layer.

question_text: (For this question use annex 081-6272A)The high lift device shown in the figure below is a
option_d: Slot or slat
explanation: The high-lift device shown is a Krueger flap, which is hinged on the lower leading edge and rotates outward and upward to increase camber.

question_text: A slat will
option_a: increase the boundary layer energy and prolongs the stall to a higher angle of attack.
option_b: increase the camber of the aerofoil and divert the flow around the sharp leading edge.
option_c: increase the lift by increasing the wing area and the camber of the aft portion of the wing.
option_d: provide a boundary layer suction on the upper side of the wing.
explanation: Slats extend from the leading edge to form a slot that channels high-pressure air over the upper surface. This slot energizes the boundary layer and postpones the stall to a higher angle of attack.

question_text: Vortex generators:
option_a: transfer energy from the free airflow into the boundary layer.
option_b: change the turbulent boundary layer into a laminar boundary layer.
option_c: reduce the spanwise flow on swept wing.
option_d: take kinetic energy out of the boundary layer to reduce separation.
explanation: Vortex generators are small vertical blades on the wing surface that create tiny vortices. These vortices mix high-energy air from the free stream into the slow-moving boundary layer, delaying flow separation.

question_text: Spoiler deflection causes :
option_a: an increase in drag and decrease in lift
option_b: an increase in lift and drag
option_d: decrease in lift and drag
explanation: Deflecting spoilers breaks up the smooth airflow over the upper surface of the wing, which causes a significant decrease in lift and a large increase in drag.

question_text: Upon extension of a spoiler on a wing:
option_a: CD is increased and CL is decreased.
option_b: only CL is decreased (CD remains unaffected).
option_c: both CL and CD are increased.
option_d: CD is increased, while CL remains unaffected.
explanation: Deploying spoilers disrupts the boundary layer and flow over the upper surface of the wing, which significantly decreases the lift coefficient and increases the drag coefficient.

question_text: When ""spoilers"" are used as speed brakes:
option_a: at same angle of attack, CD is increased and CL is decreased.
option_b: CLmax of the polar curve is not affected.
option_c: they do not affect wheel braking action during landing.
option_d: at same angle of attack, CL remains unaffected.
explanation: When spoilers are extended as speed brakes in flight, they disrupt the airflow over the wing upper surface, which decreases lift and increases aerodynamic drag at any given angle of attack.

question_text: There are two types of boundary layer: laminar and turbulent. One important advantage the turbulent boundary layer has over the laminar type is that :
option_a: it has less tendency to separate from the surface
option_d: energy is less
explanation: A turbulent boundary layer has more kinetic energy than a laminar boundary layer because of mixing. This high kinetic energy allows it to resist adverse pressure gradients and makes it less prone to flow separation.

question_text: In which phase of the take-off is the aerodynamic effect of ice located on the wing leading edge most critical?
option_a: The last part of the rotation.
option_c: During climb with all engines operating.
option_d: All phases of the take-off are equally critical.
explanation: Ice accretion on the wing leading edge is most critical during the final part of rotation because the aircraft is at a high angle of attack where the ice-distorted profile will stall prematurely.

question_text: The formula for the Mach Number is:(a= speed of sound)
option_d: M= IAS / a
explanation: Mach number (M) is a dimensionless ratio of the aircraft's True Airspeed (TAS) to the local speed of sound (a): M = TAS / a.

question_text: The Mach number:
option_a: is the ratio between the TAS of the aeroplane and the local speed of sound.
option_b: is the ratio between the TAS of the aeroplane and the speed of sound at sea level.
option_c: is the ratio between the IAS of the aeroplane and the local speed of sound.
option_d: increases at a given TAS, when the temperature rises.
explanation: Mach number is defined as the ratio between the aircraft's True Airspeed (TAS) and the local speed of sound (a) in the ambient air.

question_text: Climbing at a constant Mach Number up to FL 350 the TAS will:
option_d: remain constant.
explanation: Climbing at a constant Mach number in the standard troposphere means that as altitude increases, the temperature decreases, which decreases the local speed of sound. Consequently, the True Airspeed (TAS) must decrease.

question_text: The flight Mach number is 0.8 and the TAS is 400 kts. The speed of sound is:
option_d: 600 kts
explanation: The speed of sound (a) is calculated from the Mach number formula: a = TAS / M. For TAS = 400 kt and M = 0.8, the speed of sound is 400 / 0.8 = 500 kt.

question_text: Which statement with respect to the speed of sound is correct ?
option_a: Varies with the square root of the absolute temperature.
option_b: Increases always if the density of the air decreases.
option_d: Doubles if the temperature increases from 9° to 36° Centigrade.
explanation: The speed of sound in a gas is directly proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature in Kelvin (a = sqrt(gamma * R * T)).

question_text: If the altitude is increased and the TAS remains constant in the standard troposphere the Mach Number will:
option_d: increase or decrease, depends of the type of aeroplane.
explanation: In the standard troposphere, temperature decreases with altitude, which decreases the speed of sound. If True Airspeed (TAS) remains constant, the Mach number (M = TAS / a) must increase.

question_text: The speed of sound is affected by the:
option_d: humidity of the air.
explanation: The speed of sound in the atmosphere depends solely on the ambient air temperature, according to the equation: a = 38.94 * sqrt(T), where T is the absolute temperature in Kelvin.

question_text: An aeroplane is descending at a constant Mach number from FL 350. What is the effect on true airspeed ?
option_d: It remains constant
explanation: During a descent at a constant Mach number in the troposphere, the ambient temperature increases. Since the speed of sound is proportional to the square root of temperature, both the speed of sound and the True Airspeed (TAS) must increase.

question_text: To be able to predict compressibility effects you have to determine the:
option_d: IAS.
explanation: Compressibility effects (such as shock wave formation and wave drag) are physical phenomena that depend on the ratio of flow velocity to the speed of sound. Therefore, the Mach number is the parameter used to predict these effects.

question_text: A normal shock wave:
option_a: can occur at different points on the aeroplane in transonic flight.
option_b: is a discontinuity plane in an airflow, in which the temperature drops suddenly.
option_c: is a discontinuity plane in an airflow, in which the pressure drops suddenly.
option_d: is a discontinuity plane in an airflow, which is always normal to the surface.
explanation: A normal shock wave is a thin discontinuity plane that can form at various points on the aircraft in transonic flight. As air passes through it, the velocity drops to subsonic, and pressure, density, and temperature all rise sharply.

question_text: Which statement is correct about a normal shock wave ?
option_a: The airflow changes from supersonic to subsonic
option_c: The airflow changes from subsonic to supersonic
option_d: The airflow expands when passing the aerofoil
explanation: As airflow passes through a normal shock wave, its velocity is decelerated from supersonic to subsonic speed, while the flow direction remains perpendicular to the shock wave and does not change.

question_text: Compared with an oblique shock wave at the same Mach number a normal shock wave has a
option_d: smaller expansion.
explanation: A normal shock wave is perpendicular to the airflow, which causes a much greater deceleration and a higher compression (higher pressure increase) compared to an oblique shock wave at the same Mach number.

question_text: Compared with an oblique shock wave at the same Mach number a normal shock wave has a
option_d: lower static temperature.
explanation: Because a normal shock wave causes a larger deceleration of the flow than an oblique shock wave, it generates a greater entropy increase, which results in a higher loss in total pressure.

question_text: The regime of flight from the critical Mach number up to M = 1.3 is called the
option_d: subsonic range.
explanation: The transonic range is the flight regime extending from the critical Mach number (where the flow becomes local sonic M = 1.0 at some point) up to M = 1.3.

question_text: Mcrit is the free stream Mach Number at which:
option_a: somewhere about the airframe Mach 1 is reached locally.
option_d: the critical angle of attack is reached.
explanation: The critical Mach number (Mcrit) is the free-stream Mach number at which the local airflow velocity at some point on the aircraft's airframe (typically the upper wing surface) first reaches Mach 1.

question_text: When the Mach number is slowly increased in straight and level flight the first shockwaves will occur:
option_a: at the wing root segment, upperside.
option_b: on the underside of the wing.
option_d: somewhere on the hoizontal tail.
explanation: When the Mach number is increased, the local airflow accelerates most rapidly over the area of maximum camber, which is the upper side of the wing root segment. Thus, the first shock waves form there.

question_text: The critical Mach Number of an aeroplane is the free stream Mach Number, which produces the first evidence of :
option_d: supersonic flow.
explanation: The critical Mach number of an aeroplane is the free stream Mach number at which the local airflow velocity at some point on the airframe first reaches Mach 1.0 (local sonic flow).

question_text: Air passes a normal shock wave. Which of the following statements is correct?
option_d: The velocity increases.
explanation: As air passes through a normal shock wave, it undergoes a rapid compression. This deceleration from supersonic to subsonic speed causes a sharp increase in static pressure, density, and temperature.

question_text: The critical Mach number for an aerofoil equals the free stream airfoil Mach number at which:
option_a: sonic speed (M=1) is reached at a certain point on the upper side of the aerofoil.
option_b: the maximum operating temperature is reached.
option_c: a shock-wave appears on the upper surface.
option_d: a ""supersonic bell"" appears on the upper surface.
explanation: The critical Mach number for an aerofoil is the free-stream Mach number at which the local flow velocity at some point on the upper surface of the aerofoil first reaches Mach 1 (sonic speed).

question_text: When the air has passed through a normal shock wave the Mach number is
option_b: lower than before but still greater than 1.
option_d: higher than before.
explanation: By definition, a normal shock wave decelerates supersonic flow to a subsonic velocity. Therefore, the Mach number of the air after passing through a normal shock wave is always less than 1.

question_text: When the air is passing through a shock wave the static temperature will
option_d: decrease and beyond a certain Mach number start increasing again
explanation: Passing through a shock wave causes a sudden compression and deceleration of the airflow, which converts kinetic energy into thermal energy and increases the static temperature.

question_text: When the air is passing through a shock wave the density will
option_d: decrease and beyond a certain Mach number start increasing again
explanation: A shock wave is a compression wave. As the airflow passes through it, the air decelerates and compresses, which causes the density to increase.

question_text: When air has passed through a shock wave the speed of sound is
option_d: decreased and beyond a certain Mach number start increasing again
explanation: As air passes through a shock wave, the static temperature increases. Since the speed of sound is directly proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature, the speed of sound behind the shock wave is increased.

question_text: Just above the critical Mach number the first evidence of a shock wave will appear at the
option_d: trailing edge of the wing.
explanation: When an aircraft exceeds its critical Mach number, the local flow first becomes supersonic on the upper surface of the wing (where the camber is greatest). Consequently, the first shock wave forms on the upper side of the wing.

question_text: Critical Mach-number is the :
option_a: highest speed without supersonic flow over any part of the aeroplane.
option_b: speed at which there is subsonic airflow over all parts of the aircraaeroplane Mach number < 1).
option_c: speed at which there is supersonic airflow over all parts of the aeroplane.
option_d: highest speed at which the aeroplane is certificated for operation (MMO).
explanation: The critical Mach number is the highest free-stream Mach number at which there is no supersonic flow over any part of the aeroplane.

question_text: The loss of total pressure in a shock wave is due to the fact that
option_a: kinetic energy in the flow is changed into heat energy.
option_b: the speed reduction is too high.
option_c: the static pressure decrease is comparatively high.
option_d: the friction in the boundary layer is higher.
explanation: A shock wave is a highly irreversible thermodynamic process. The loss in total pressure is due to the conversion of kinetic energy in the flow into heat energy (entropy increase).

question_text: Which of the following (1) aerofoils and (2) angles of attack will produce the lowest Mcrit values?
option_d: (1) thin and (2) small.
explanation: Thick aerofoils and high angles of attack both cause a larger acceleration of the local airflow over the upper surface. This causes the local flow to reach Mach 1 at a lower free-stream speed, producing the lowest critical Mach number (Mcrit).

question_text: In the transonic range the aeroplane characteristics are strongly determined by:
option_d: the CAS.
explanation: In the transonic range, the aerodynamic characteristics of the aircraft (such as drag rise and center of pressure shift) are heavily determined by compressibility effects, which are a function of the Mach number.

question_text: Which of the following flight phenomena can happen at Mach Numbers below the critical Mach Number?
option_d: Shock stall.
explanation: Dutch roll is a lateral-directional oscillation that can occur at any speed, including subsonic Mach numbers below the critical Mach number. Tuck under, Mach buffet, and shock stall require shock wave formation above Mcrit.

question_text: The critical Mach Number of an aeroplane can be increased by:
option_d: dihedral of the wings.
explanation: Sweeping the wings back reduces the effective velocity component perpendicular to the leading edge. This delays the local flow acceleration to Mach 1, thereby increasing the critical Mach number.

question_text: In transonic flight the ailerons will be less effective than in subsonic flight because:
option_a: aileron deflection only partly affects the pressure distribution around the wing.
option_b: behind the shock wave pressure is lower.
option_c: aileron down deflection moves the shock wave forward.
option_d: aileron deflection only affects the air in front of the shock wave.
explanation: In transonic flight, shock waves form on the wing surfaces. Because pressure disturbances cannot travel forward through supersonic flow, deflecting an aileron behind a shock wave only affects the pressure distribution behind the shock, reducing its overall effectiveness.

question_text: Two methods to increase the critical Mach Number are:
option_a: thin aerofoils and sweep back of the wing.
option_b: thin aerofoils and dihedral of the wing.
option_c: positive cambering of the aerofoil and sweep back of the wing.
option_d: thick aerofoils and dihedral of the wing.
explanation: To delay the onset of local supersonic flow and increase the critical Mach number, aircraft designs utilize thin aerofoils (low thickness-to-chord ratio) and swept-back wing configurations.

question_text: If an aeroplane is flying at transonic speed with increasing Mach number the shock wave on the upper side of the wing
option_c: stays all the time at the same position.
option_d: disappears.
explanation: As the flight Mach number increases in the transonic range, the local supersonic region expands aft, causing the shock wave on the upper surface to move aft towards the trailing edge.

question_text: To increase the critical Mach number a conventional aerofoil should
option_a: have a low thickness to chord ratio.
option_c: be used with a high angle of attack.
option_d: have a large leading edge radius.
explanation: To increase the critical Mach number, a wing profile should have a low thickness-to-chord ratio (thin aerofoil), which minimizes the local acceleration of the airflow over the upper surface.

question_text: The critical Mach number can be increased by
option_d: an increase in wing aspect ratio.
explanation: Sweeping the wings back reduces the effective chordwise component of the airflow velocity, which delays the onset of supersonic flow and increases the critical Mach number.

question_text: Some aeroplanes have a 'waist' or 'coke bottle' contoured fuselage. This is done to
option_b: increase the strength of the wing root junction.
option_c: fit the engine intakes better to the fuselage.
option_d: improve the low speed characteristics.
explanation: The coke-bottle shaped fuselage contour is designed to satisfy the transonic Area Rule. This rule minimizes wave drag by ensuring a smooth distribution of the aircraft's cross-sectional area from nose to tail.

question_text: The application of the area rule on aeroplane design will decrease the
option_d: form drag.
explanation: The Area Rule states that the wave drag of an aircraft is minimized when the cross-sectional area distribution is smooth. Applying this rule (such as designing a fuselage waist) significantly decreases transonic wave drag.

question_text: When comparing a rectangular wing and a swept back wing of the same wing area and wing loading, the swept back wing has the advantage of :
option_d: Lower stalling speed
explanation: For a given wing area and wing loading, a swept-back wing reduces the effective flow velocity perpendicular to the leading edge, which increases the critical Mach number compared to a rectangular wing.

question_text: What is the influence of decreasing aeroplane weight on Mcrit at constant IAS ?
option_a: Mcrit increases as a result of flying at a smaller angle of attack.
option_b: Mcrit increases as a result of compressibility effects.
option_d: Mcrit decreases as a result of flying at a greater angle of attack.
explanation: A lower aircraft weight reduces the lift required to maintain level flight. The aircraft can fly at a smaller angle of attack and lower lift coefficient, which reduces the suction peak on the upper wing surface and increases Mcrit.

question_text: What is the effect of a decreasing aeroplane weight on Mcrit at n=1, when flying at constant IAS ? The value of Mcrit:
option_c: is independent of the angle of attack.
option_d: decreases.
explanation: A decrease in aircraft weight reduces the required lift. This allows the aircraft to operate at a lower lift coefficient and angle of attack, reducing local flow acceleration and increasing Mcrit.

question_text: How does stalling speed (IAS) vary with altitude?
option_a: It remains constant at lower altitudes but increases at higher altitudes due to compressibility effects.
option_c: It increases with increasing altitude, because the density decreases.
option_d: It remains constant at lower altitudes but decreases at higher altitudes due to compressibility effects.
explanation: Stalling speed (IAS) remains constant at lower altitudes. However, at high altitudes, compressibility effects reduce CLmax, which causes the indicated stalling speed to increase.

question_text: Which kind of flow separation occurs at the smallest angle of attack?
option_d: deep stall.
explanation: Shockstall (shock-induced stall) can occur at small angles of attack if the Mach number is high enough to form strong shock waves that cause boundary layer separation.

question_text: At higher altitudes, the stall speed (IAS):
option_d: decreases until the tropopause
explanation: At high altitudes (especially above FL250), compressibility effects become significant and degrade the aerodynamic efficiency of the wing, which reduces CLmax and increases the indicated stall speed (IAS).

question_text: Shock stall is:
option_a: separation of the boundary layer behind the shock wave.
option_b: separation of the flow behind the bow wave.
option_c: separation of the flow at high angles of attack and at high Mach Numbers.
option_d: separation of the flow at the trailing edge of the wing at high Mach Numbers.
explanation: Shockstall is the separation of the boundary layer immediately behind a shock wave, which is caused by the strong adverse pressure gradient of the shock wave at high Mach numbers.

question_text: Which of the following flight phenomena can only happen at Mach Numbers above the critical Mach Number?
option_d: Elevator stall.
explanation: Mach buffet is caused by boundary layer separation behind shock waves, which can only form when the flight Mach number exceeds the critical Mach number.

question_text: Shock induced separation results in
option_d: decreasing drag.
explanation: Shock-induced boundary layer separation disrupts the smooth airflow over the upper wing surface. This results in a rapid decrease in lift and a significant increase in drag.

question_text: In the transonic range lift will decrease at the shock stall due to the
option_a: separation of the boundary layer at the shock waves.
option_b: attachment of the shock wave on the trailing edge of the wing.
option_c: first appearance of a shock wave at the upper side of the wing.
option_d: appearance of the bow wave.
explanation: During a shock stall in the transonic range, the strong adverse pressure gradient of the shock wave causes the boundary layer to separate, leading to a sudden decrease in lift.

question_text: The high speed buffet is induced by
option_a: boundary layer separation due to shock waves.
option_c: expansion waves on the wing upper side.
option_d: a shift of the centre of gravity.
explanation: High-speed buffet is a violent vibration caused by the turbulent wake of flow separation immediately behind the shock waves on the upper surface of the wing.

question_text: ""Tuck under"" is caused by (i) which movement of the centre of pressure of the wing and (ii) which change of the downwash angle at the location of the stabilizer.
option_d: (i) forward (ii) increasing
explanation: Tuck under is a nose-down pitching tendency caused by (i) the center of pressure shifting aft as the supersonic region expands, and (ii) a decrease in the downwash angle at the horizontal tail due to flow separation on the wing root.

question_text: The consequences of exceeding Mcrit in a swept-wing aeroplane may be : (assume no corrective devices, straight and level flight)
option_a: buffeting of the aeroplane and a tendency to pitch down.
option_b: an increase in speed and a tendency to pitch up.
option_d: buffeting of the aeroplane and a tendency to pitch up.
explanation: Exceeding the critical Mach number causes shock wave formation and flow separation. This results in aerodynamic buffeting of the aircraft and a strong nose-down pitching moment (tuck under).

question_text: The Mach trim system will:
option_a: adjust the stabilizer, depending on the Mach Number.
option_b: keep the Mach Number automatically constant.
option_c: pump the fuel from tank to tank, depending on the Mach Number.
option_d: adjust the elevator trim tab, depending on the Mach Number.
explanation: A Mach trim system is an automatic system that adjusts the stabilizer angle (or elevator) as a function of the Mach number to counteract the tuck-under nose-down pitching moment.

question_text: The Mach trim system will prevent:
option_d: shock stall.
explanation: The Mach trim system is designed to automatically apply nose-up trim as the Mach number increases, preventing the dangerous nose-down pitching moment known as tuck under.

question_text: When an aeroplane is flying through the transonic range with increasing Mach Number the centre of the pressure of the wing will move aft. This requires:
option_a: a pitch up input of the stabilizer.
option_c: much more thrust from the engine.
option_d: a higher IAS to compensate the nose down effect.
explanation: As the center of pressure shifts aft in the transonic range, it creates a nose-down moment. To maintain balance, the Mach trim system must automatically provide a nose-up input to the horizontal stabilizer.

question_text: Tuck under will happen
option_a: only above the critical Mach number.
option_b: only at the critical Mach number.
option_c: only below the critical Mach number.
option_d: above or below the critical Mach number depending on the angle of attack.
explanation: Tuck under is caused by shock wave formation and boundary layer separation, which can only happen at Mach numbers above the critical Mach number.

question_text: The Mach-trim function is installed on most commercial jets in order to minimize the adverse effects of :
option_a: changes in the position of centre of pressure
option_b: increased drag due to shock wave formation
option_d: compressibility effects on the stabilizer
explanation: The Mach-trim system is installed to automatically counteract the nose-down pitching moment (tuck under) caused by the aft movement of the center of pressure in the transonic range.

question_text: (For this question use annex 081-1331A)An A 310 aeroplane weighing 100 tons is turning at FL 350 at constant altitude with a bank of 50 degrees. Its flight Mach range between low-speed buffeting and high-speed buffeting goes from:
explanation: Using the A310 Buffet Onset Boundary chart for a weight of 100 tons and a 50-degree banked turn at FL350 (which increases the load factor n = 1.56), the buffet-free Mach range is from M = 0.69 to M higher than 0.84.

question_text: What data may be obtained from the Buffet Onset Boundary chart?
option_a: The values of the Mach Number at which low speed and Mach Buffet occur at different weights and altitudes.
option_b: The values of MMO at different weights and altitudes.
option_c: The values of Mcrit at different weights and altitudes.
option_d: The values of the Mach Number at which low speed and shock-stall occur at different weights and altitudes.
explanation: The Buffet Onset Boundary chart plots the Mach number against pressure altitude for various aircraft weights, showing the boundaries where low-speed buffet (stalling) and high-speed buffet (shock stall) occur.

question_text: The maximum acceptable cruising altitude is limited by a minimum acceptable loadfactor because exceeding that altitude:
option_b: turbulence may exceed the limit load factor.
option_c: a sudden necessary bankangle may exceed the limit load factor.
option_d: Mach buffet will occur immediately.
explanation: Exceeding the maximum cruising altitude narrows the buffet margin. In this region (known as Coffin Corner), even minor turbulence can induce a load factor spike that triggers Mach buffet.

question_text: Should a transport aeroplane fly at a higher Mach number than the 'buffet-onset' Mach number?
option_d: Yes, if you want to fly fast at very high altitudes.
explanation: Flying at a Mach number higher than the buffet-onset Mach number is not acceptable, as it causes severe aerodynamic buffeting, structural fatigue, and loss of control due to shock-induced flow separation.

question_text: A jet aeroplane is cruising at high altitude with a Mach-number, that provides a buffet margin of 0.3g incremental. In order to increase the buffet margin to 0.4g incremental the pilot must :
option_a: fly at a lower altitude and the same Mach-number
option_b: extend the flaps to the first selection
option_d: fly at a larger angle of attack
explanation: To increase the buffet margin (which increases the speed range between low-speed and high-speed buffet), the aircraft must operate in denser air, which is achieved by flying at a lower altitude.

question_text: The buffet margin :
option_a: increases during a descent with a constant IAS.
option_b: is always greatest after a stepclimb has been executed.
option_c: decreases during a descent with a constant Mach number.
option_d: is always positive at Mach numbers below MMO.
explanation: During a descent at a constant Indicated Airspeed (IAS), the air density increases and the Mach number decreases. This decreases the lift coefficient required for level flight and increases the margin to both low-speed and high-speed buffet, thereby increasing the overall buffet margin.

question_text: Vortex generators on the upper side of the wing surface will:
option_a: decrease the intensity of shock wave induced air separation.
option_c: decrease the span wise flow at high Mach Numbers.
option_d: increase the magnitude of the shock wave.
explanation: Vortex generators form small, high-energy vortices that mix the boundary layer with the free stream. This energizes the boundary layer and decreases the intensity of shock wave induced flow separation.

question_text: Vortex generators on the upper side of the wing:
option_d: decrease critical Mach Number.
explanation: Although vortex generators increase parasite drag slightly, they delay shock-induced boundary layer separation, which decreases the wave drag and total drag at high Mach numbers.

question_text: Vortex generators mounted on the upper wing surface will
option_a: decrease the shock wave induced separation.
option_b: decrease the interference drag of the trailing edge flaps.
option_c: decrease the stalling speed by increase of the tangential velocity of the swept wing.
option_d: increase the effectiveness of the spoiler due to increase in parasite drag.
explanation: Vortex generators on the upper wing surface energize the boundary layer, which delays flow separation immediately behind the shock waves and decreases shock wave induced boundary layer separation.

question_text: How will the density and temperature change in a supersonic flow from a position in front of a shock wave to behind it ?
option_a: Density will increase, temperature will increase.
option_b: Density will increase, temperature will decrease.
option_c: Density will decrease, temperature will increase.
option_d: Density will decrease, temperature will decrease.
explanation: As air passes through a shock wave, the sudden compression causes both the density of the air and the static temperature of the air to increase.

question_text: At what speed does the front of a shock wave move across the earth's surface?
option_a: The ground speed of the aeroplane.
option_b: The speed of sound at ground level.
option_c: The speed of sound at flight level.
option_d: The true air speed of the aeroplane.
explanation: The shock wave moves with the aircraft. Therefore, the front of the shock wave moves across the earth's surface at the ground speed of the aeroplane.

question_text: In supersonic flight, all disturbances produced by an aeroplane are:
option_a: in between a conical area, depending on the Mach Number.
option_b: outside the conical area depending on the Mach Number.
option_d: very weak and negligible.
explanation: In supersonic flight, pressure disturbances cannot travel ahead of the aircraft. All disturbances are confined within a conical region trailing behind the aircraft, known as the Mach cone, whose angle depends on the Mach number.

question_text: The bow wave will appear first at:
explanation: The bow wave is a detached shock wave that forms at the nose of the aircraft when the flight speed becomes fully supersonic (Mach 1.0).

question_text: If the Mach number of an aeroplane in supersonic flight is increased, the shock wave angles will
option_d: decrease and beyond a certain Mach number start increasing again.
explanation: As the flight Mach number in supersonic flight increases, the angle of the shock waves (Mach angle) decreases according to the relation: sin(mu) = 1 / M.

question_text: When air has passed an expansion wave, the static pressure is:
option_b: decreased or increased, depending on Mach Number.
option_d: unchanged.
explanation: An expansion wave is the opposite of a shock wave. As airflow passes through an expansion wave, it accelerates, causing the static pressure, temperature, and density to decrease.

question_text: When the air is passing through an expansion wave the local speed of sound will
option_d: decrease and beyond a certain Mach number start increasing again.
explanation: As air passes through an expansion wave, it accelerates and its static temperature decreases. Since the speed of sound is proportional to the square root of the static temperature, the local speed of sound decreases.

question_text: When the air is passing through an expansion wave the Mach number will
option_d: decrease and beyond a certain Mach number start increasing again.
explanation: As airflow passes through an expansion wave, the flow accelerates, which causes the local Mach number to increase.

question_text: When the air is passing through an expansion wave the static temperature will
option_d: decrease and beyond a certain Mach number start increasing again.
explanation: An expansion wave accelerates and expands the airflow, which causes the static temperature of the air to decrease.

question_text: In case of supersonic flow retarded by a normal shock wave a high efficiency (low loss in total pressure) can be obtained if the Mach number in front of the shock is
option_d: exactly 1.
explanation: A normal shock wave is most efficient (causes the lowest loss in total pressure) when the Mach number immediately in front of it is only slightly supersonic (just above Mach 1).

question_text: Which statement is correct about an expansion wave in a supersonic flow ?1- The density in front of an expansion wave is higher than behind.2- The pressure in front of an expansion wave is higher than behind.
option_d: 1 and 2 are incorrect.
explanation: As air passes through an expansion wave, the flow expands and accelerates, which means the density and static pressure of the air in front of the expansion wave are higher than behind it.

question_text: Which statement is correct about an expansion wave in supersonic flow ?1. The temperature in front of an expansion wave is higher than the temperature behind it.2. The speed in front of an expansion wave is higher than the speed behind it.
option_d: 1 and 2 are incorrect.
explanation: As air passes through an expansion wave, it accelerates and expands. This means the temperature in front of the expansion wave is higher than behind it (statement 1 is correct), but the velocity in front is lower than behind it (statement 2 is incorrect).

question_text: On a non swept wing, when the aerofoil is accelerated from subsonic to supersonic speeds, the aerodynamic centre :
option_a: shifts from 25% to about 50% of the aerofoil chord.
option_d: slightly shifts forward.
explanation: On a non-swept wing, accelerating from subsonic to supersonic speed causes the aerodynamic center to shift aft from the 25% chord position (quarter-chord) to approximately the 50% chord position (mid-chord).

question_text: If an aeroplane is accelerated from subsonic to supersonic speeds, the centre of pressure will move:
option_c: to a position near the leading edge.
option_d: to a position near the trailing edge.
explanation: As an aircraft accelerates through the transonic range to supersonic speeds, the shock waves move aft and the pressure distribution becomes more uniform, shifting the center of pressure aft to approximately the 50% chord position.

question_text: The aft movement of the centre of pressure during the acceleration through the transonic flight regime will:
option_d: decrease the static lateral stability.
explanation: The aft movement of the center of pressure during transonic acceleration increases the distance between the CG and the center of pressure. This increases the aircraft's static longitudinal stability (making it more stable but harder to pitch up).

question_text: In supersonic flight aerofoil pressure distribution is:
option_d: the same as in subsonic flight.
explanation: In subsonic flight, the wing pressure distribution is peak-shaped near the leading edge. In supersonic flight, the pressure distribution is uniform and can be modeled as a rectangular distribution.

question_text: If a symmetrical aerofoil is accelerated from subsonic to supersonic speed the centre of lift will move
option_d: forward to the mid chord.
explanation: As a symmetrical aerofoil accelerates from subsonic to supersonic speeds, the aerodynamic center and the center of lift shift aft from the 25% chord position to the 50% chord position (mid-chord).

question_text: The additional increase of drag at Mach Numbers above the critical Mach Number is due to:
option_d: increased skin friction.
explanation: At Mach numbers above the critical Mach number, shock waves form on the aircraft. The additional drag rise is caused by wave drag, which is the energy lost in generating these shock waves.

question_text: If the total sum of moments about one of its axis is not zero, an aeroplane:
option_a: would experience an angular acceleration about that axis.
option_c: would fly a path with a constant curvature.
option_d: would not be affected because the situation is normal.
explanation: According to Newton's laws of rotation, if the sum of aerodynamic and thrust moments about an axis is not zero, the aircraft must experience an angular acceleration about that axis.

question_text: In which situation would the wing lift of an aeroplane in straight and level flight have the highest value ?
option_a: Forward centre of gravity and idle thrust.
option_b: Aft centre of gravity and idle thrust.
option_c: Forward centre of gravity and take-off thrust.
option_d: Aft centre of gravity and take-off thrust.
explanation: Wing lift must balance the aircraft's weight plus any downward tail load. A forward center of gravity requires a large downward tail load to balance the nose-heavy pitching moment, which increases the required wing lift.

question_text: If the sum of moments in flight is not zero, the aeroplane will rotate about:
option_b: the neutral point of the aeroplane.
option_c: the aerodynamic centre of the wing.
option_d: the centre of pressure of the wing.
explanation: An aircraft in free flight is not constrained by a physical hinge. Therefore, any unbalanced moments will cause the aircraft to rotate about its center of gravity.

question_text: When an aeroplane with the centre of gravity forward of the centre of pressure of the combined wing / fuselage is in straight and level flight, the vertical load on the tailplane will be:
option_c: zero because in steady flight all loads are in equilibrium.
option_d: downwards because it is always negative regardless of the position of the centre of gravity.
explanation: When the CG is forward of the wing's center of pressure, the aircraft is nose-heavy. To maintain pitching equilibrium, the horizontal stabilizer must generate a downward vertical load.

question_text: An aeroplane, with a C.G. location behind the centre of pressure of the wing can only maintain a straight and level flight when the horizontal tail loading is:
option_d: upwards or downwards depending on elevator deflection.
explanation: If the CG is located behind the wing's center of pressure, the aircraft is tail-heavy. To maintain pitch equilibrium in level flight, the horizontal tailplane must generate an upward aerodynamic force.

question_text: In a twin-engined jet powered aeroplane (engines mounted below the low wings) the thrust is suddenly increased. Which elevator deflection will be required to maintain the pitching moment zero ?
option_c: No elevator movement will required because the thrust line of the engines remains unchanged.
option_d: It depends on the position of the centre of gravity.
explanation: Engines mounted below the wing create a thrust line below the CG, which produces a nose-up pitching moment when thrust is increased. To maintain equilibrium, the pilot must deflect the elevator down to create a balancing nose-down moment.

question_text: Which of the following statements is correct?
option_a: Dynamic stability is possible only when the aeroplane is statically stable about the relevant axis.
option_b: Static stability means that the aeroplane is also dynamically satble about the relevant axis.
option_c: Dynamic stability means that after being displaced from original equilibrium condition, the aeroplane will return to that condition without oscillation.
option_d: A dynamically stable aeroplane would be almost impossible to fly manually.
explanation: An aircraft cannot be dynamically stable unless it is first statically stable. Static stability provides the initial restoring force, while dynamic stability dictates how the resulting oscillations damp out over time.

question_text: Positive static stability of an aeroplane means that once it has been displaced the :
option_a: initial tendency to move is towards its equilibrium position.
option_b: initial tendency to move is away from its equilibrium position.
option_c: tendency will be to move with an oscillating motion of decreasing amplitude.
option_d: tendency will be to move with an oscillating motion of increasing amplitude.
explanation: Static stability is the initial tendency of an aircraft. Positive static stability means that after a disturbance, the initial force generated will tend to return the aircraft to its original equilibrium position.

question_text: After a disturbance about the lateral axis, an aeroplane oscillates about the lateral axis at a constant amplitude. The aeroplane is:
option_d: Statically unstable - Dynamically neutral
explanation: Statically stable means there is a restoring force. Dynamically neutral means the resulting oscillations do not increase or decrease in amplitude, remaining constant over time.

question_text: Which one of the following statements about the dynamic stability of a conventional aeroplane about the lateral axis is correct?
option_a: Damping of the phugoid is normally very weak.
option_b: Speed remains constant during one period of the phugoid.
option_c: Period time of the phugoid is normally 5 sec.
option_d: An aft C.G. position shortens the period time of the phugoid.
explanation: The phugoid (long-period mode) is a slow pitch oscillation where the aircraft exchanges altitude for speed. Because it involves very little pitching motion, horizontal tail damping is weak, and the damping is normally very weak.

question_text: The ""short period mode"" is an:
option_d: unstable movement of the aeroplane, induced by the pilot.
explanation: The short-period mode is a rapid, heavily damped pitch oscillation about the lateral axis that occurs immediately after a disturbance, before the aircraft's speed has time to change.

question_text: An aeroplane that has positive static stability:
option_a: can be dynamically stable, neutral or unstable.
option_d: is always dynamically unstable.
explanation: Positive static stability only guarantees that there is a restoring force. Depending on the aerodynamic damping, the resulting motion can be dynamically stable (damped), neutral (constant amplitude), or unstable (divergent).

question_text: A statically unstable aeroplane is:
option_d: sometimes dynamically unstable.
explanation: If an aircraft is statically unstable, it lacks any restoring force to return to equilibrium. Without a restoring force, it will diverge immediately and can never be dynamically stable.

question_text: One of the requirements for dynamic stability is:
option_b: a large deflection range of the stabilizer trim.
option_d: effective elevator.
explanation: Dynamic stability refers to the damping of oscillations. Since oscillations require an initial restoring force, positive static stability is a fundamental prerequisite for dynamic stability.

question_text: The manoeuvrability of an aeroplane is best when the:
option_a: C.G. is on the aft C.G. limit.
option_c: C.G. position is on the forward C.G. limit.
option_d: flaps are down.
explanation: Manouevrability is the ease with which the aircraft's flight path can be changed. When the CG is at the aft limit, the static margin is minimized, reducing stability and making the aircraft highly maneuverable with light control forces.

question_text: Longitudinal static stability is created by the fact that the:
option_a: centre of gravity is located in front of the neutral point of the aeroplane.
option_b: centre of gravity is located in front of the leading edge of the wing.
option_c: wing surface is greater than the horizontal tail surface.
option_d: aeroplane possesses a large trim speed range.
explanation: Longitudinal static stability requires a restoring moment when the angle of attack changes. This is achieved when the center of gravity is located ahead of the aircraft's neutral point.

question_text: The aerodynamic centre of the wing is the point, where:
option_a: pitching moment coefficient does not vary with angle of attack.
option_b: change of lift due to variation of angle of attack is constant.
option_d: the aeroplane's lateral axis intersects with the centre of gravity.
explanation: The aerodynamic center (AC) of a wing is the point along the chord line where the pitching moment coefficient remains constant and does not vary with changes in the angle of attack.

question_text: For a normal stable aeroplane, the centre of gravity is located:
option_a: with a sufficient minimum margin ahead of the neutral point of the aeroplane.
option_b: aft of the neutral point of the aeroplane.
option_c: at the neutral point of the aeroplane.
option_d: between the aft limit and the neutral point of the aeroplane.
explanation: For a conventional stable aircraft, the center of gravity must be located with a safe minimum margin (the static margin) ahead of the aircraft's neutral point.

question_text: The max aft position of the centre of gravity is amongst others limited by the:
option_a: minimum value of the stick force per g.
option_b: maximum longitudinal stability of the aeroplane.
option_d: too small effect of the controls on the aeroplane.
explanation: As the CG moves aft, the static longitudinal stability decreases. The maximum aft CG limit is set to ensure that the stick force per g (maneuver stability) does not drop below a safe minimum value.

question_text: A C.G location beyond the aft limit leads to:
option_a: an unacceptable low value of the manoeuvre stability (stick force per g, Fe/g).
option_b: a too high pulling stick force during rotation in the take off.
option_d: a better recovery performance in the spin.
explanation: A CG position behind the aft limit reduces the static margin below safe limits, resulting in an unacceptably low stick force per g (maneuver stability), which makes the aircraft dangerously over-sensitive to control inputs.

question_text: In what way is the longitudinal stability affected by the degree of positive camber of the aerofoil?
option_a: No effect, because camber of the aerofoil produces a constant pitch down moment coefficient, independent of angle of attack.
option_b: Positive, because the centre of pressure shifts rearward at increasing angle of attack.
option_c: Negative, because the lift vector rotates forward at increasing angle of attack.
option_d: Positive, because the lift vector rotates backward at increasing angle of attack.
explanation: Camber does not affect the slope of the lift curve or the aerodynamic center. It only produces a constant pitch-down moment coefficient (independent of angle of attack), meaning it has no effect on longitudinal stability.

question_text: Which part of an aeroplane provides the greatest positive contribution to the static longitudinal stability ?
option_d: The wing.
explanation: The horizontal tailplane is located far behind the CG, creating a long moment arm. When the angle of attack changes, the tailplane generates a large restoring lift force, making the greatest positive contribution to static longitudinal stability.

question_text: During landing of a low-winged jet aeroplane, the maximum elevator up deflection is normally required when the flaps are:
option_a: fully down and the C.G. is fully forward.
option_b: up and the C.G. is fully forward.
option_c: fully down and the C.G. is fully aft.
option_d: up and the C.G. is fully aft.
explanation: During landing, the combination of fully extended flaps (which create a large nose-down moment) and a forward CG (which makes the aircraft nose-heavy) requires the maximum nose-up elevator deflection (elevator up) to flare.

question_text: The C.G. position of an aeroplane is forward of the neutral point in a fixed location. Speed changes cause a departure from the trimmed position. Which of the following statements about the stick force stability is correct?
option_a: Increasing 10 kt trimmed at low speed has more effect on the stick force than increasing 10 kt trimmed at high speed.
option_b: Increase of speed generates pull forces.
option_c: Aeroplane nose up trim decreases the stick force stability.
option_d: Stick force stability is not affected by trim.
explanation: Stick force stability is a measure of the control force required to change speed from trim. Because dynamic pressure is higher at high speeds, a 10 kt change at low speed requires a larger pitch control deflection and has a more noticeable effect on stick force.

question_text: ""Tuck under"" is:
option_a: the tendency to nose down when speed is increased into the transonic flight regime.
option_b: the tendency to nose up when speed is increased into the transonic flight regime.
option_c: shaking of the control column at high Mach Number.
option_d: the tendency to nose down when the control column is pulled back.
explanation: Tuck under is the automatic tendency of an aircraft to pitch nose-down when its speed is increased into the transonic flight regime, caused by the aft shift of the center of pressure.

question_text: ""Tuck under"" may happen at:
option_d: only at low altitudes.
explanation: Tuck under is a compressibility effect caused by shock wave formation and the aft shift of the center of pressure, which only occurs at high transonic Mach numbers.

question_text: Which of the following statements about a Mach trimmer is correct?
option_a: A Mach trimmer corrects the change in stick force stability of a swept wing aeroplane above a certain Mach number.
option_b: A straight wing aeroplane always needs a Mach trimmer for flying at Mach numbers close to MMO.
option_c: A Mach trimmer reduces the stick force stability of a straight wing aeroplane to zero at high Mach numbers.
option_d: The Mach trimmer corrects the natural tendency of a swept wing aeroplane to pitch-up.
explanation: A Mach trimmer is an automatic control system that adjusts the horizontal stabilizer to compensate for the reduction in stick force stability (tuck under) that swept-wing aeroplanes experience at high Mach numbers.

question_text: In case the Mach trimmer fails:
option_a: the Mach number must be limited.
option_b: try to relocate the centre-of-gravity aft.
option_c: the speed must be kept constant.
option_d: the aeroplane weight must be limited.
explanation: If the Mach trimmer fails in flight, the aeroplane's maximum operating speed must be restricted to a lower Mach number to ensure the pilot does not encounter uncontrollable tuck under.

question_text: A Machtrimmer:
option_a: corrects insufficient stick force stability at high Mach Numbers.
option_b: increases the stick force per g at high Mach Numbers.
option_c: is necessary for compensation of the autopilot at high Mach Numbers.
option_d: has no effect on the shape of the elevator position versus speed (IAS) curve for a fully hydraulic controlled aeroplane.
explanation: The primary purpose of a Mach trimmer is to automatically correct the reduction in stick force stability (tuck under tendency) that occurs at high Mach numbers in swept-wing aeroplanes.

question_text: The (1) stick force stability and the (2) manoeuvre stability are positively affected by:
option_a: (1) forward C.G. position (2) forward CG. position.
option_b: (1) forward C.G. position (2) aeroplane nose up trim.
option_c: (1) aft C.G. position (2) aft CG. position.
option_d: (1) aeroplane nose up trim (2) aeroplane nose up trim.
explanation: Both stick force stability (speed stability) and maneuver stability are positively affected by a forward center of gravity (CG) position, which increases the static margin and requires larger pilot control inputs for pitching.

question_text: Which statement about stick force per g is correct?
option_a: The stick force per g must have both an upper and lower limit in order to assure acceptable control characteristics.
option_b: The stick force per g increases, when centre of gravity is moved aft.
option_c: The stick force per g can only be corrected by means of electronic devices (stability augmentation) in case of an unacceptable value.
option_d: If the slope of the Fe-n line becomes negative, generally speaking this is not a problem for control of an aeroplane.
explanation: The stick force per g (maneuver stability) must be within certified upper and lower limits. If it is too low, the aircraft is oversensitive and easy to overstress; if it is too high, the pilot cannot maneuver effectively.

question_text: The value of the manoeuvre stability of an aeroplane is 150 N/g. The load factor in straight and level flight is 1. The increase of stick force necessary to achieve the load factor of 2.5 is:
explanation: The maneuver stability is 150 N/g. The change in load factor is delta-n = 2.5 - 1.0 = 1.5 g. The required increase in stick force is: Force = Manoeuvre Stability * delta-n = 150 * 1.5 = 225 N.

question_text: An aeroplane has static directional stability, in a side-slip to the right, initially the:
option_a: nose of the aeroplane tends to move to the right.
option_b: right wing tends to go down.
option_c: nose of the aeroplane will remain in the same direction.
option_d: nose of the aeroplane tends to move to the left.
explanation: When an aeroplane sideslips to the right, the relative wind strikes the fuselage and vertical tail from the right. Positive static directional stability (weathercock stability) generates a yawing moment that turns the nose of the aeroplane to the right, into the relative wind.

question_text: The effect of a positive wing sweep on static directional stability is as follows:
option_d: Negative dihedral effect
explanation: Positive wing sweepback contributes to static directional stability because the advancing wing presents a larger frontal area and lower sweep relative to the airflow, producing more drag and a restoring yawing moment.

question_text: The effect of a high wing with zero dihedral is as follows:
option_c: Its only purpose is to ease aeroplane loading
option_d: Zero dihedral effect
explanation: A high-wing configuration creates a positive dihedral effect (lateral stability) during a sideslip because the airflow passes around the fuselage and generates high pressure underneath the windward wing, rolling the aircraft away from the sideslip.

question_text: Which of the following lists aeroplane features that each increase static lateral stability ?
option_a: High wing, sweep back, large and high vertical fin.
option_b: Low wing, dihedral, elliptical wing planform.
option_d: Sweep back, under wing mounted engines, winglets.
explanation: Aeroplane design features that increase static lateral stability (effective dihedral) include a high wing position, swept-back wings, and a large vertical fin (which also provides directional stability).

question_text: Which type of wing arrangement decreases the static lateral stability of an aeroplane?
option_d: Increased wing span.
explanation: An anhedral wing arrangement (wings slanted downwards) decreases the static lateral stability (effective dihedral effect). It is often used on high-wing aircraft to prevent excessive lateral stability and Dutch roll.

question_text: The effect of a ventral fin on the static stability of an aeroplane is as follows : (1=longitudinal, 2=lateral, 3=directional)
option_d: 1 : no effect, 2 : positive, 3: negative
explanation: A ventral fin is mounted underneath the rear fuselage. It has no effect on longitudinal stability, creates a small negative dihedral effect (decreases lateral stability) because its center of pressure is below the roll axis, and increases directional stability by acting as additional vertical fin area.

question_text: Dihedral of the wing:
option_b: is the only way to increase the static lateral stability.
option_c: is only positive for aeroplanes with high mounted wings.
option_d: decreases the static lateral stability.
explanation: Geometric dihedral (tilting the wings upward) increases the static lateral stability (effective dihedral) by ensuring the low wing in a sideslip operates at a higher angle of attack and produces more lift, which rolls the aircraft back to level.

question_text: Which statement is correct for a side slip condition at constant speed and side slip angle, where the geometric dihedral of an aeroplane is increased ?
option_a: the required lateral control force increases.
option_b: the required lateral control force decreases.
option_c: the required lateral control force does not change.
option_d: the stick force per g decreases.
explanation: Increasing the geometric dihedral increases the aircraft's static lateral stability. In a sideslip, this generates a stronger restoring rolling moment, which requires the pilot to apply larger lateral control forces (aileron input) to maintain the sideslip angle.

question_text: Which of the following statements about dihedral is correct?
option_a: The ""effective dihedral"" of an aeroplane component means the contribution of that component to the static lateral stability.
option_b: Effective dihedral is the angle between the 1/4-chord line and the lateral axis of the aeroplane.
option_c: Dihedral contributes to dynamic but not to static lateral stability.
option_d: Dihedral is necessary for the execution of slip-free turns.
explanation: The term 'effective dihedral' refers to the total contribution of all aircraft components (such as wing sweep, wing position, and geometric dihedral) to the static lateral stability.

question_text: Which of the following statements about static lateral and directional stability is correct?
option_a: An aeroplane with an excessive static directional stability in relation to its static lateral stability, will be prone to spiral dive. (spiral instability)
option_b: The effects of static lateral and static directional stability are completely independent of each other because they take place about different axis.
option_c: An aeroplane with an excessive static directional stability in relation to its static lateral stability, will be prone to ""Dutch roll"".
option_d: Static directional stability can be increased by installing more powerful engines.
explanation: An aeroplane with excessive static directional stability relative to its static lateral stability will tend to yaw quickly into a slip, which increases the lift on the outer wing and rolls the aircraft into a steeper turn, leading to a spiral dive.

question_text: Sensitivity for spiral dive will occur when :
option_a: the static directional stability is positive and the static lateral stability is relatively weak.
option_b: the static directional stability is negative and the static lateral stability is positive.
option_c: the static lateral and directional stability are both negative.
option_d: the dutch roll tendency is too strongly suppressed by the yaw damper.
explanation: Spiral instability (sensitivity to a spiral dive) occurs when the aircraft's static directional (weathercock) stability is strong and its static lateral stability (effective dihedral) is relatively weak.

question_text: Which one of the following systems suppresses the tendency to ""Dutch roll""?
option_d: Rudder limiter.
explanation: A yaw damper is an active automatic system that senses yaw rate and applies rapid, coordinated rudder inputs to suppress the lateral-directional oscillation known as Dutch roll.

question_text: Which aeroplane behaviour will be corrected by a yaw damper ?
option_d: Buffeting.
explanation: A yaw damper is designed to automatically detect and damp out the lateral-directional oscillations of Dutch roll by applying counter-rudder deflections.

question_text: What will increase the sensitivity to Dutch Roll?
option_c: A forward movement of the centre of gravity.
option_d: An increased anhedral.
explanation: Dutch roll is a lateral-directional oscillation that is aggravated by a strong lateral stability (effective dihedral) and a weak directional stability. Therefore, increasing the static lateral stability increases the sensitivity to Dutch roll.

question_text: With increasing altitude and constant IAS the static lateral stability (1) and the dynamic lateral/directional stability (2) of an aeroplane with swept-back wing will:
option_d: (1) decrease (2) increase.
explanation: At constant IAS and higher altitudes, the true airspeed is higher. This increases the lift curve slope and sweepback contribution, which increases static lateral stability (1). However, because air density is lower, aerodynamic damping of the tail is reduced, causing the dynamic lateral/directional stability (2) to decrease.

question_text: Rotation about the lateral axis is called :
option_d: slipping.
explanation: Rotation about the lateral axis of the aircraft (pitch axis) is called pitching.

question_text: Rolling is the rotation of the aeroplane about the:
option_d: wing axis.
explanation: Rolling is the aerodynamic rotation of the aircraft about its longitudinal axis (roll axis).

question_text: What is the effect on the aeroplane's static longitudinal stability of a shift of the centre of gravity to a more aft location and on the required control deflection for a certain pitch up or down?
option_a: The static longitudinal stability is smaller and the required control deflection is smaller.
option_b: The static longitudinal stability is larger and the required control deflection is smaller.
option_c: The static longitudinal stability is larger and the required control deflection is larger.
option_d: The static longitudinal stability is smaller and the required control deflection is larger.
explanation: Shifting the CG aft decreases the static margin, which decreases the static longitudinal stability. Because the stability is reduced, the required control deflection to achieve a given pitch change becomes smaller (controls are more sensitive).

question_text: The centre of gravity moving aft will:
option_c: not affect the elevator up or down effectiveness.
option_d: increase or decrease the elevator up effectiveness, depending on wing location.
explanation: Moving the CG aft reduces the nose-heavy pitching moment, which decreases the tail downforce required for pitch equilibrium and increases the elevator up effectiveness during pitching maneuvers.

question_text: In a mechanically controlled aeroplane, the most forward allowable position of the centre of gravity could be limited by the:
option_d: wing surface, stabilizer surface.
explanation: The most forward center of gravity limit is restricted by elevator capability and control forces. The pilot must have sufficient elevator authority and acceptable control forces to rotate during takeoff and flare during landing.

question_text: When the C.G. position is moved forward, the elevator deflection for a manoeuvre with a load factor greater than 1 will be:
option_d: dependent on trim position.
explanation: Moving the CG forward increases the static margin, making the aircraft more nose-heavy. To perform a maneuver with a load factor greater than 1 (pulling g), the pilot must apply a larger elevator deflection to overcome the increased stability.

question_text: An advantage of locating the engines at the rear of the fuselage, in comparison to a location beneath the wing, is :
option_a: less influence on longitudinal control of thrust changes.
option_c: a wing which is less sensitive to flutter.
option_d: lighter wing construction.
explanation: Mounting the engines at the rear of the fuselage aligns the thrust line closer to the center of gravity, which minimizes the pitching moment changes (longitudinal control influence) when thrust settings are adjusted.

question_text: What happens during an engine failure with two similar aeroplanes with wing mounted engines, one of them with jet engines, the other one with co-rotating propellers:
option_a: More roll tendency for the propeller aeroplane.
option_b: The same yaw tendency for both aeroplanes regardless of left or right engine failure.
option_c: The same roll tendency for both aeroplanes.
option_d: Less roll tendency for the propeller aeroplane.
explanation: For a propeller-driven aircraft with wing-mounted engines, the slipstream and torque effects are asymmetric. An engine failure will produce more roll tendency compared to a jet aircraft, where the thrust line is clean.

question_text: A jet aeroplane equipped with inboard and outboard ailerons is cruising at its normal cruise Mach number. In this case
option_a: only the inboard ailerons are active.
option_b: only the outboard aileron are active.
option_c: the inboard and outboard ailerons are active.
option_d: only the spoilers will be active, not the ailerons.
explanation: At high Mach numbers and normal cruise speeds, outboard ailerons are locked out (de-activated) to prevent high wing-bending moments and structural twisting (aileron reversal), so only the inboard ailerons are active.

question_text: Flaperons are controls which are used simultaneously as
option_d: flaps and elevator.
explanation: Flaperons are multi-functional flight control surfaces that combine the functions of ailerons (roll control) and flaps (lift augmentation).

question_text: When are outboard ailerons (if present) de-activated ?
option_a: Flaps (and slats) retracted or speed above a certain value.
option_b: Flaps (and/or slats) extended or speed below a certain value..
option_d: Landing gear extended.
explanation: Outboard ailerons are de-activated (locked out) when the flaps are retracted and the aircraft accelerates above a certain speed, preventing structural twisting and wing flutter.

question_text: During initiation of a turn with speedbrakes extended, the roll spoiler function induces a spoiler deflection:
option_a: downward on the upgoing wing and upward on the downgoing wing.
option_b: upward on the upgoing wing and downward on the downgoing wing.
option_d: on the downgoing wing only.
explanation: When spoilers are extended as speed brakes, entering a turn causes the roll spoiler function to retract the spoilers on the upgoing wing (downward deflection) and further extend them on the downgoing wing (upward deflection) to produce a rolling moment.

question_text: Differential aileron deflection:
option_a: equals the drag of the right and left aileron.
option_b: is required to keep the total lift constant when ailerons are deflected.
option_d: is required to achieve the required roll-rate.
explanation: Differential aileron deflection is a design feature where the upgoing aileron deflects further than the downgoing aileron. This is used to balance the aerodynamic drag of both sides and counteract adverse yaw.

question_text: An example of differential aileron deflection during initiation of left turn is:
option_d: Left aileron: 2° downRight aileron: 5° up
explanation: Differential aileron deflection means the upward deflecting aileron moves through a larger angle than the downward deflecting one. In a left turn, the left aileron goes up (e.g., 5° up) and the right goes down (e.g., 2° down).

question_text: How is adverse yaw compensated for during entry into and roll out from a turn ?
option_d: Servo tabs
explanation: Adverse yaw is caused by the higher induced drag on the wing with the downward-deflected aileron. It is compensated for by using differential aileron deflection, where the upgoing aileron deflects further than the downgoing one.

question_text: One method to compensate adverse yaw is a
option_d: balance panel.
explanation: Differential ailerons are designed to deflect upwards through a larger angle than downwards, which increases drag on the inside wing of a turn to compensate for adverse yaw.

question_text: Which of the following statements concerning control is correct?
option_a: In a differential aileron control system the control surfaces have a larger upward than downward maximum deflection.
option_b: On some aeroplanes, the servo tab also serves as a trim tab.
option_c: Hydraulically powered control surfaces do not need mass balancing.
option_d: In general the maximum downward elevator deflection is larger than upward.
explanation: Differential aileron systems are designed to have a larger upward maximum deflection than downward deflection to counteract adverse yaw.

question_text: Which phenomenon is counteracted with differential aileron deflection?
option_d: Turn co-ordination.
explanation: Differential ailerons are designed to counteract the adverse yaw that occurs when the downward-deflected aileron on the outer wing generates more induced drag than the upward-deflected aileron.

question_text: If the nose of an aeroplane yaws to port (left), this causes:
option_b: a decrease in relative airspeed on the starboard (right) wing.
option_c: an increase in lift on the port (left) wing.
option_d: a roll to starboard (right).
explanation: Yawing to the left causes the right wing to travel faster than the left wing, generating more lift on the right wing and rolling the aircraft to the left (port).

question_text: Which moments or motions interact in a dutch roll?
option_d: Pitching and adverse yaw.
explanation: Dutch roll is a dynamic lateral-directional oscillation that involves a combination of rolling and yawing motions.

question_text: Which statement is correct about a spring tab ?
option_a: At high IAS it behaves like a servo tab
option_b: At low IAS it behaves like a servo tab
option_c: At high IAS it behaves like a fixed extension of the elevator
option_d: Its main purpose is to increase stick force per g
explanation: A spring tab is a control tab that incorporates a spring. At high IAS, the aerodynamic force on the elevator is high, so the control input compresses the spring and the tab behaves like a servo tab to reduce control forces. At low IAS, it acts as a rigid control extension.

question_text: Which kind of ''tab'' is commonly used in case of manual reversion of fully powered flight controls ?
option_d: Anti-balance tab
explanation: A servo tab is commonly used in manual reversion flight control systems because the aerodynamic force on the tab helps deflect the main control surface when hydraulic pressure is lost.

question_text: An aeroplane has a servo-tab controlled elevator. What will happen when only the elevator jams during flight ?
option_c: The servo-tab now works as a negative trim-tab.
option_d: The pitch control forces double.
explanation: If the main elevator jams, deflecting the cockpit control column still moves the servo tab. The tab's deflection generates an aerodynamic force that moves the tail, but because the main control is jammed, the control direction is reversed (pitch control reverses direction).

question_text: A horn balance in a control system has the following purpose:
option_d: to decrease the effective longitudinal dihedral of the aeroplane.
explanation: A horn balance is a portion of the control surface that extends ahead of the hinge line. It uses aerodynamic force on the horn to assist in deflecting the control, which decreases stick forces.

question_text: Which statement about a primary control surface controlled by a servo tab, is correct ?
option_a: The position is undetermined during taxiing, in particular with tailwind.
option_b: The servo tab can also be used as a trimtab.
option_c: The control effectiveness of the primary surface is increased by servo tab deflection.
option_d: Due to the effectiveness of the servo tab the control surface area can be smaller.
explanation: A servo-tab controlled surface is aerodynamically free. During taxiing at low speeds (especially with a tailwind), there is insufficient airflow to hold the controls, so the surface position is undetermined.

question_text: Examples of aerodynamic balancing of control surfaces are:
option_a: seal between wing's trailing edge and leading edge of a control surface, horn balance
option_b: upper and lower rudder, seal between wing's trailing edge and leading edge of a control surface
option_c: weight in the nose of the control surface, horn balance
option_d: Fowler flaps, upper and lower rudder
explanation: Aerodynamic balancing is used to reduce control force. Examples include a horn balance (portion of the surface ahead of the hinge) and a seal between the wing's trailing edge and the leading edge of a control surface (internal balance).

question_text: Examples of aerodynamic balancing of control surfaces are:
option_a: servo tab, spring tab, seal between the wing trailing edge and the leading edge of control surface.
option_b: balance tab, horn balance, and mass balance.
option_c: mass in the nose of the control surface, horn balance and mass balance.
option_d: spring tab, servo tab, and power assisted control.
explanation: Aerodynamic balancing methods include balance tabs, spring tabs, servo tabs, horn balances, and seals between the wing trailing edge and the control surface leading edge.

question_text: elevator deflection, dynamic pressure.
explanation: The control force in a manual system is determined by the elevator deflection and the dynamic pressure of the airflow.

question_text: When power assisted controls are used for pitch control, this:
option_a: ensures that a part of the aerodynamic forces is still felt on the column.
option_c: makes aerodynamic balancing of the control surfaces meaningless.
option_d: can only function in combination with an elevator trim tab.
explanation: Power-assisted control systems use hydraulic actuators to assist the pilot's inputs. A feedback mechanism is installed to ensure that a portion of the aerodynamic control force is still felt on the control column, providing artificial feel.

question_text: When flutter damping of control surfaces is obtained by mass balancing, these weights will be located with respect to the hinge of the control surface:
option_d: behind the hinge.
explanation: To prevent flutter, mass balancing weights are installed on the control surfaces ahead of (in front of) the hinge line, which shifts the center of gravity of the control surface forward onto or ahead of the hinge axis.

question_text: What is the position of the elevator in relation to the trimmable horizontal stabilizer of a power assisted aeroplane, which is in trim ?
option_a: The position depends on speed, the position of slats and flaps and the position of the centre of gravity.
option_b: The elevator deflection (compared to the stabilizer position) is always zero.
option_c: At a forward CG the elevator is deflected upward and at an aft CG the elevator is deflected downward.
option_d: The elevator is always deflected slightly downwards in order to have sufficient remaining flare capability.
explanation: In a power-assisted control system with a trimmable horizontal stabilizer (THS), once the aircraft is trimmed, the elevator deflection relative to the stabilizer is zero to minimize drag.

question_text: How would the exterior appearance of an aeroplane change, when trimming for speed increase ?
option_a: Elevator deflection is increased further downward by an upward deflected trim tab
option_b: The elevator is deflected further up by a downward deflected trim tab
option_c: The elevator is deflected further downward by means of a movable horizontal stabiliser
option_d: The exterior appearance of the aeroplane will not change
explanation: Trimming for a speed increase requires the aircraft to be trimmed nose-down. This is achieved by deflecting the trim tab upward, which forces the elevator to deflect downward, nose-down.
